c1.label: Q1
c1.prompt: Where is the light sensor that this program reads?

B.text: In the sonar module at the front

c1.why: The 25 red LEDs work backwards as well — they can measure the light falling on them. The sensor is on the micro:bit, not the car.

c2.label: Q2

B.text: On or off, like a switch

C.text: Yes or no — light or dark

c2.why: It is a number, which is why you have to pick a line to split it at. Where you put that line is your decision.

c3.label: Q3
c3.prompt: Your friend copies your threshold of 10 and their headlights never come on. Why?

A.text: Their room is brighter than yours

c3.why: A threshold belongs to a room, not to a program. Theirs has to be measured where they are.

r1.label: Q1
r1.prompt: You cover the micro:bit with your hand. What happens?
r1.why: Covering it drops the light level below 10, so the test is true and the lights switch on.

r2.label: Q2
r2.prompt: What color do the headlights show?
r2.why: Red, green and blue all at full make white. Mixing is what these three numbers are for.

r3.label: Q3
r3.prompt: You cover the sensor, then uncover it. What do the headlights do?

B.text: Come on, then go out again

r3.why: There is no `else`, so nothing ever turns them off. Switching something on is only half the job.

r4.label: Q4
r4.prompt: What is the car doing while the lights switch themselves on and off?

A.text: Driving only when it is dark

B.text: Stopping each time the lights change

r4.why: The drive block runs once at start-up and nothing cancels it. The loop only decides about the lights.

d1.label: Q1
d1.prompt: The headlights are on in daylight and go out when it gets dark — backwards. Which change fixes it?

D.text: Add a pause inside each branch

d1.why: `>` asks "is it bright?". The car should light up when it is dark, so the test has to point the other way.

d2.label: Q2
d2.prompt: The lights are decided once at start-up and never change again. What is missing?

C.text: A pause between the two branches

d2.why: A sensor has to be asked over and over. Asked once, the answer is stuck at whatever the room was at start-up.

b1.label: Q1
b1.prompt: Each time round the loop, in what order does the program do these? 1 test whether it is below your threshold · 2 read the light level · 3 turn the lights on or off · 4 go back to the top and do it again
b1.why: Read, test, act — then repeat it forever. The loop goes round the finished decision, not before it.

b2.label: Q2
b2.prompt: You measure your room and get readings around 120 in daylight and around 30 with the lights off. Which threshold is sensible?
b2.why: A threshold works best between the two readings, not on top of one of them. Sitting exactly on 30 makes the lights flicker.
